tools.name: configuration_view
tools.description: Get the current Kubernetes configuration content as a kubeconfig YAML

minified.description: Return a minified version of the configuration. If set to true, keeps only the current-context and the relevant pieces of the configuration for that context. If set to false, all contexts, clusters, auth-infos, and users are returned in the configuration. (Optional, default true)

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: helm_install
tools.description: Install (deploy) a Helm chart to create a release in the current or provided namespace

chart.description: Chart reference to install (for example: stable/grafana, oci://ghcr.io/nginxinc/charts/nginx-ingress)

name.description: Name of the Helm release (Optional, random name if not provided)

namespace.description: Namespace to install the Helm chart in (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

values.description: Values to pass to the Helm chart (Optional)

tools.name: helm_list
tools.description: List all the Helm releases in the current or provided namespace (or in all namespaces if specified)

all_namespaces.description: If true, lists all Helm releases in all namespaces ignoring the namespace argument (Optional)

namespace.description: Namespace to list Helm releases from (Optional, all namespaces if not provided)

tools.name: helm_uninstall
tools.description: Uninstall a Helm release in the current or provided namespace

name.description: Name of the Helm release to uninstall

namespace.description: Namespace to uninstall the Helm release from (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Nodes or all nodes in the cluster

What I changed
- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - replicas: 2
  - container: rec-engine
  - containerPort: 80
  - security configuration matches engine-v2-0 (no additional pod/container securityContext)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select all pods with app=recommendation-engine (removed version filter) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1. Left targetPort as 8080 (unchanged from the existing Service).

Current state
- engine-v2-0: 2/2 ready
- engine-v2-1: 2/2 ready
- With the Service now selecting both, traffic will be distributed roughly evenly per pod; with 2 pods on each Deployment this yields about 50/50 canary vs stable.

Adjustments and rollback
- To change traffic weight, adjust replicas (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary ≈ 75/25).
- To rollback quickly, either:
  - revert the Service selector to add version: v2.0, or
  - scale engine-v2-1 to 0 replicas, or
  - delete engine-v2-1.

namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done.

What I changed
- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - replicas: 2
  - container: rec-engine

Current state
- engine-v2-0: 2/2 ready
- engine-v2-1: 2/2 ready
- With the Service now selecting both, traffic will be distributed roughly evenly per pod; with 2 pods on each Deployment this yields about 50/50 canary vs stable.

Adjustments and rollback
- To change traffic weight, adjust replicas (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary ≈ 75/25).
- To rollback quickly, either:
  - revert the Service selector to add version: v2.0, or
  - scale engine-v2-1 to 0 replicas, or
  - delete engine-v2-1.

- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29

Current state
- engine-v2-0: 2/2 ready
- engine-v2-1: 2/2 ready
- With the Service now selecting both, traffic will be distributed roughly evenly per pod; with 2 pods on each Deployment this yields about 50/50 canary vs stable.

Adjustments and rollback
- To change traffic weight, adjust replicas (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary ≈ 75/25).
- To rollback quickly, either:
  - revert the Service selector to add version: v2.0, or
  - scale engine-v2-1 to 0 replicas, or
  - delete engine-v2-1.

outputSteps.content:
I found the cause and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment overrode the container entrypoint with:
  - command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
  - args: ["nonexistent_command"]
- This made the container exit immediately and caused CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed
- Removed the custom command/args so the nginx image runs with its default entrypoint.

Current status
- A new ReplicaSet was created and the Pod is healthy:
  - crashloop-test/app-57fc6cc69b-9pqrl: 1/1 Running
- Events show normal pull/start; no more BackOff.

If you want a custom startup command, tell me what it should run and I’ll add it safely (and include proper probes).

Notes:
- No data loss occurred since the original PVC never bound to a volume.
- If you intended to use a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or need a different size, I can update the claim accordingly.

outputSteps.content:
All set. I fixed the issue and your pod is now running.

What I found and did:
- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc" (event: pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims).
- Fix: Recreated the PVC using the available StorageClass "standard" (minikube hostpath). The PVC immediately Bound.
- Result: homepage-pod in homepage-ns is now Running and Ready.

Notes:
- No data loss occurred since the original PVC never bound to a volume.
- If you intended to use a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or need a different size, I can update the claim accordingly.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but the Deployment’s probes and the Service were using port 80 and custom paths (/is_ready, /get_status). That caused connection refused and failing readiness/liveness.

What I changed
- Deployment (orders/webapp):
  - Set container port name http on 8080.
  - Updated readiness and liveness probes to GET / on port 8080.
- Service (orders/webapp):
  - Point targetPort to the named container port http (8080).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Running.
- Deployment is Available=True with 1 ready replica.
- Service endpoints point to port 8080 and are ready.

How to verify
- Port-forward: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080
- In-cluster DNS: http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local

There’s no Ingress defined for external access. If you want, I can create an Ingress (or OpenShift Route) with TLS.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but the Deployment’s probes and the Service were using port 80 and custom paths (/is_ready, /get_status). That caused connection refused and failing readiness/liveness.

What I changed
- Deployment (orders/webapp):
  - Set container port name http on 8080.
  - Updated readiness and liveness probes to GET / on port 8080.
- Service (orders/webapp):
  - Point targetPort to the named container port http (8080).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Running.
- Deployment is Available=True with 1 ready replica.
- Service endpoints point to port 8080 and are ready.

How to verify
- Port-forward: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080
- In-cluster DNS: http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local

There’s no Ingress defined for external access. If you want, I can create an Ingress (or OpenShift Route) with TLS.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but the Deployment’s probes and the Service were using port 80 and custom paths (/is_ready, /get_status). That caused connection refused and failing readiness/liveness.

What I changed
- Deployment (orders/webapp):
  - Set container port name http on 8080.
  - Updated readiness and liveness probes to GET / on port 8080.
- Service (orders/webapp):
  - Point targetPort to the named container port http (8080).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Running.
- Deployment is Available=True with 1 ready replica.
- Service endpoints point to port 8080 and are ready.

How to verify
- Port-forward: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080
- In-cluster DNS: http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local

There’s no Ingress defined for external access. If you want, I can create an Ingress (or OpenShift Route) with TLS.

pod/webapp-7d8467cb84-lgzv5 condition met

Current readiness probe path: /
Success: Both probe paths have been fixed
Success: Pod is stable with acceptable number of restarts

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader only allowed listing Deployments (apps/v1) and did not grant any permissions on Pods (core API group). That’s why listing pods returned “forbidden.”

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include read permissions on Pods:
  - apiGroup: "" (core)
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Kept the existing permission to list Deployments.

It’s fixed now
- The pod-reader ServiceAccount in simple-rbac-setup can now list pods in that namespace.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup
- Or try listing: kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- If you ever need to list pods across multiple namespaces, use a ClusterRole and a ClusterRoleBinding instead of a namespaced Role/RoleBinding.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader only allowed listing Deployments (apps/v1) and did not grant any permissions on Pods (core API group). That’s why listing pods returned “forbidden.”

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include read permissions on Pods:
  - apiGroup: "" (core)
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Kept the existing permission to list Deployments.

It’s fixed now
- The pod-reader ServiceAccount in simple-rbac-setup can now list pods in that namespace.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup
- Or try listing: kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- If you ever need to list pods across multiple namespaces, use a ClusterRole and a ClusterRoleBinding instead of a namespaced Role/RoleBinding.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The nginx pod is running in web (labels: app=nginx).
- The Service web/nginx had:
  - selector: app=web (did not match the pod’s label), so Endpoints were empty → no traffic to any pod.
  - targetPort: 80, but the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080, so even with endpoints, traffic to port 80 would fail.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated the Service to select the correct pods and forward to the correct container port:
  - selector: app: nginx
  - ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

Verification
- Endpoints now show the nginx pod and port:
  - web/nginx → 10.244.0.27:8080
- From a test pod inside the cluster:
  - nslookup nginx.web.svc.cluster.local → 10.100.138.219
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local → HTTP/1.1 200 OK and HTML returned.

Notes/next steps
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s only reachable inside the cluster. If you need external access, I can:
  - create an Ingress, or
  - change the Service to NodePort/LoadBalancer (depending on your environment).
- I left a temporary debug pod web/curl-tester running for verification. Say the word and I’ll remove it.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The nginx pod is running in web (labels: app=nginx).
- The Service web/nginx had:
  - selector: app=web (did not match the pod’s label), so Endpoints were empty → no traffic to any pod.
  - targetPort: 80, but the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080, so even with endpoints, traffic to port 80 would fail.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated the Service to select the correct pods and forward to the correct container port:
  - selector: app: nginx
  - ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

Verification
- Endpoints now show the nginx pod and port:
  - web/nginx → 10.244.0.27:8080
- From a test pod inside the cluster:
  - nslookup nginx.web.svc.cluster.local → 10.100.138.219
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local → HTTP/1.1 200 OK and HTML returned.

Notes/next steps
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s only reachable inside the cluster. If you need external access, I can:
  - create an Ingress, or
  - change the Service to NodePort/LoadBalancer (depending on your environment).
- I left a temporary debug pod web/curl-tester running for verification. Say the word and I’ll remove it.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The nginx pod is running in web (labels: app=nginx).
- The Service web/nginx had:
  - selector: app=web (did not match the pod’s label), so Endpoints were empty → no traffic to any pod.
  - targetPort: 80, but the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080, so even with endpoints, traffic to port 80 would fail.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated the Service to select the correct pods and forward to the correct container port:
  - selector: app: nginx
  - ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

Verification
- Endpoints now show the nginx pod and port:
  - web/nginx → 10.244.0.27:8080
- From a test pod inside the cluster:
  - nslookup nginx.web.svc.cluster.local → 10.100.138.219
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local → HTTP/1.1 200 OK and HTML returned.

Notes/next steps
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s only reachable inside the cluster. If you need external access, I can:
  - create an Ingress, or
  - change the Service to NodePort/LoadBalancer (depending on your environment).
- I left a temporary debug pod web/curl-tester running for verification. Say the word and I’ll remove it.

results.taskOutput:
Here’s what I found and what I fixed.

Diagnosis
- Pods stuck Pending: Events showed FailedScheduling: “didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.” The Deployment had nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label, so nothing could schedule.
- Connection refused: The service web-app-service pointed to targetPort: 80, but the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 by default. So even once pods run, the service would send traffic to the wrong port and fail.

What I changed
- Removed the bad nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (so pods can schedule on the available node).
- Updated the Service to targetPort: 8080 so it matches the container’s listening port.

Current state
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-lsdft (10.244.0.32)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-zjvbb (10.244.0.33)
- Service endpoints: populated with both pods, now serving on port 8080.
- Verification: In-pod curl to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK.

Impact for your frontend
- The DNS name web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local is correct; with the fix in place, connections should now succeed.

Recommendations (optional hardening)
- If you intended to schedule on special nodes, add that label to the node and then reintroduce nodeSelector:
  - kubectl label node <your-node> environment=production-gpu
- Align the Deployment containerPort to 8080 (metadata only, but less confusing) and add probes:
  - readinessProbe: httpGet path: /, port: 8080
  - livenessProbe: httpGet path: /, port: 8080

Let me know if you want me to add the probes and adjust containerPort as a follow-up.

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Here’s what I found and what I fixed.

Diagnosis
- Pods stuck Pending: Events showed FailedScheduling: “didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.” The Deployment had nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label, so nothing could schedule.
- Connection refused: The service web-app-service pointed to targetPort: 80, but the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 by default. So even once pods run, the service would send traffic to the wrong port and fail.

What I changed
- Removed the bad nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (so pods can schedule on the available node).
- Updated the Service to targetPort: 8080 so it matches the container’s listening port.

Current state
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-lsdft (10.244.0.32)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-zjvbb (10.244.0.33)
- Service endpoints: populated with both pods, now serving on port 8080.
- Verification: In-pod curl to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK.

Impact for your frontend
- The DNS name web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local is correct; with the fix in place, connections should now succeed.

Recommendations (optional hardening)
- If you intended to schedule on special nodes, add that label to the node and then reintroduce nodeSelector:
  - kubectl label node <your-node> environment=production-gpu
- Align the Deployment containerPort to 8080 (metadata only, but less confusing) and add probes:
  - readinessProbe: httpGet path: /, port: 8080
  - livenessProbe: httpGet path: /, port: 8080

Let me know if you want me to add the probes and adjust containerPort as a follow-up.

outputSteps.content:
Here’s what I found and what I fixed.

Diagnosis
- Pods stuck Pending: Events showed FailedScheduling: “didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.” The Deployment had nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label, so nothing could schedule.
- Connection refused: The service web-app-service pointed to targetPort: 80, but the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 by default. So even once pods run, the service would send traffic to the wrong port and fail.

What I changed
- Removed the bad nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (so pods can schedule on the available node).
- Updated the Service to targetPort: 8080 so it matches the container’s listening port.

Current state
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-lsdft (10.244.0.32)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-zjvbb (10.244.0.33)
- Service endpoints: populated with both pods, now serving on port 8080.
- Verification: In-pod curl to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK.

Impact for your frontend
- The DNS name web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local is correct; with the fix in place, connections should now succeed.

Recommendations (optional hardening)
- If you intended to schedule on special nodes, add that label to the node and then reintroduce nodeSelector:
  - kubectl label node <your-node> environment=production-gpu
- Align the Deployment containerPort to 8080 (metadata only, but less confusing) and add probes:
  - readinessProbe: httpGet path: /, port: 8080
  - livenessProbe: httpGet path: /, port: 8080

Let me know if you want me to add the probes and adjust containerPort as a follow-up.

Done.

I created the Pod communication-pod in the multi-container-logging namespace with:
- Two containers under spec.containers:
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, serving on port 8080, readinessProbe httpGet / on port 8080

- A shared volume logs-volume (emptyDir) mounted at /var/log/nginx in both containers
- Pod readiness tied to the web-server readiness (via the readiness probe)

How to verify:
- kubectl get pod communication-pod -n multi-container-logging
- kubectl logs communication-pod -c logger -n multi-container-logging
- kubectl port-forward pod/communication-pod 8080:8080 -n multi-container-logging and curl http://localhost:8080/

I created the Pod communication-pod in the multi-container-logging namespace with:

- Pod readiness tied to the web-server readiness (via the readiness probe)

- kubectl get pod communication-pod -n multi-container-logging

- kubectl port-forward pod/communication-pod 8080:8080 -n multi-container-logging and curl http://localhost:8080/

results.taskOutput:
I’ve set up the multi-tenant development environment as requested. Summary of what’s been created and how it meets each requirement:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled each namespace (ns=<name>, plus purpose/tenant/owner) to support NetworkPolicies.

2) RBAC
- Full access per developer to their own namespace:
  - RoleBindings in each dev namespace binding:
    - User alice → ClusterRole admin in dev-alice
    - User bob → ClusterRole admin in dev-bob
    - User charlie → ClusterRole admin in dev-charlie
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding Users alice, bob, charlie to ClusterRole view
- Service accounts:
  - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
  - Each SA bound to ClusterRole admin in its own namespace
  - Each SA bound to ClusterRole view in dev-shared
- Staging and prod:
  - No developer bindings. Access remains only for cluster admins (default allow via cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding to system:masters).

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi, requests.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi, requests.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi, requests.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all six non-system namespaces.
- Allow DNS and system services for all namespaces:
  - Egress to kube-dns/coredns on UDP/TCP 53
  - General egress to any pod in kube-system (for system services)
- Developer traffic scoping:
  - In dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
    - Allow traffic within same namespace (Ingress/Egress)
    - Allow traffic to and from dev-shared only
    - Cross-developer traffic is blocked
- dev-shared:
  - Allow within same namespace
  - Allow traffic to/from dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- staging and prod:
  - Fully isolated from dev namespaces:
    - Only same-namespace traffic allowed (Ingress/Egress)
    - DNS/system-services egress allowed
    - No paths from/to dev namespaces
- System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) not modified.

5) Default Deny Policies
- Implemented default deny Ingress and Egress in all created namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod). System namespaces are untouched.

Notes and verification tips
- NetworkPolicy enforcement requires a CNI that supports it (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea).
- Verify:
  - kubectl get ns
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get sa,rolebinding,resourcequota,networkpolicy
    (repeat for other namespaces)
- Connectivity checks:
  - From a pod in one dev namespace, curls to another dev namespace Service/Pod IP should be blocked.
  - Access to dev-shared from dev namespaces should succeed.
  - Access from any namespace to DNS (UDP/TCP 53) and kube-system services should succeed.
- If developers need in-cluster Kubernetes API access (https://kubernetes.default.svc), we can optionally allow egress to the API service IP via an IPBlock rule; let me know and I can add it using your cluster’s Service IP for “kubernetes” in the default namespace.

If you’d like, I can also:
- Create LimitRanges for default CPU/memory requests/limits per namespace.
- Provide kubeconfigs or tokens for the developer service accounts.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

I’ve set up the multi-tenant development environment as requested. Summary of what’s been created and how it meets each requirement:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled each namespace (ns=<name>, plus purpose/tenant/owner) to support NetworkPolicies.

2) RBAC
- Full access per developer to their own namespace:
  - RoleBindings in each dev namespace binding:
    - User alice → ClusterRole admin in dev-alice
    - User bob → ClusterRole admin in dev-bob
    - User charlie → ClusterRole admin in dev-charlie
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding Users alice, bob, charlie to ClusterRole view
- Service accounts:
  - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
  - Each SA bound to ClusterRole admin in its own namespace
  - Each SA bound to ClusterRole view in dev-shared
- Staging and prod:
  - No developer bindings. Access remains only for cluster admins (default allow via cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding to system:masters).

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi, requests.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi, requests.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi, requests.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all six non-system namespaces.
- Allow DNS and system services for all namespaces:
  - Egress to kube-dns/coredns on UDP/TCP 53
  - General egress to any pod in kube-system (for system services)
- Developer traffic scoping:
  - In dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
    - Allow traffic within same namespace (Ingress/Egress)
    - Allow traffic to and from dev-shared only
    - Cross-developer traffic is blocked
- dev-shared:
  - Allow within same namespace
  - Allow traffic to/from dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- staging and prod:
  - Fully isolated from dev namespaces:
    - Only same-namespace traffic allowed (Ingress/Egress)
    - DNS/system-services egress allowed
    - No paths from/to dev namespaces
- System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) not modified.

5) Default Deny Policies
- Implemented default deny Ingress and Egress in all created namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod). System namespaces are untouched.

Notes and verification tips
- NetworkPolicy enforcement requires a CNI that supports it (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea).
- Verify:
  - kubectl get ns
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get sa,rolebinding,resourcequota,networkpolicy
    (repeat for other namespaces)
- Connectivity checks:
  - From a pod in one dev namespace, curls to another dev namespace Service/Pod IP should be blocked.
  - Access to dev-shared from dev namespaces should succeed.
  - Access from any namespace to DNS (UDP/TCP 53) and kube-system services should succeed.
- If developers need in-cluster Kubernetes API access (https://kubernetes.default.svc), we can optionally allow egress to the API service IP via an IPBlock rule; let me know and I can add it using your cluster’s Service IP for “kubernetes” in the default namespace.

If you’d like, I can also:
- Create LimitRanges for default CPU/memory requests/limits per namespace.
- Provide kubeconfigs or tokens for the developer service accounts.

outputSteps.content:
I’ve set up the multi-tenant development environment as requested. Summary of what’s been created and how it meets each requirement:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled each namespace (ns=<name>, plus purpose/tenant/owner) to support NetworkPolicies.

2) RBAC
- Full access per developer to their own namespace:
  - RoleBindings in each dev namespace binding:
    - User alice → ClusterRole admin in dev-alice
    - User bob → ClusterRole admin in dev-bob
    - User charlie → ClusterRole admin in dev-charlie
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding Users alice, bob, charlie to ClusterRole view
- Service accounts:
  - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
  - Each SA bound to ClusterRole admin in its own namespace
  - Each SA bound to ClusterRole view in dev-shared
- Staging and prod:
  - No developer bindings. Access remains only for cluster admins (default allow via cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding to system:masters).

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi, requests.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi, requests.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi, requests.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all six non-system namespaces.
- Allow DNS and system services for all namespaces:
  - Egress to kube-dns/coredns on UDP/TCP 53
  - General egress to any pod in kube-system (for system services)
- Developer traffic scoping:
  - In dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
    - Allow traffic within same namespace (Ingress/Egress)
    - Allow traffic to and from dev-shared only
    - Cross-developer traffic is blocked
- dev-shared:
  - Allow within same namespace
  - Allow traffic to/from dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- staging and prod:
  - Fully isolated from dev namespaces:
    - Only same-namespace traffic allowed (Ingress/Egress)
    - DNS/system-services egress allowed
    - No paths from/to dev namespaces
- System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) not modified.

5) Default Deny Policies
- Implemented default deny Ingress and Egress in all created namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod). System namespaces are untouched.

Notes and verification tips
- NetworkPolicy enforcement requires a CNI that supports it (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea).
- Verify:
  - kubectl get ns
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get sa,rolebinding,resourcequota,networkpolicy
    (repeat for other namespaces)
- Connectivity checks:
  - From a pod in one dev namespace, curls to another dev namespace Service/Pod IP should be blocked.
  - Access to dev-shared from dev namespaces should succeed.
  - Access from any namespace to DNS (UDP/TCP 53) and kube-system services should succeed.
